did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the heading of the prophecy: “A message from the LORD” to Israel, delivered “through Malachi.”
The LORD declares his love for Israel, but the people ask how he has shown that love.
To illustrate the distinction he made between Jacob and Esau, the LORD reminds them that Jacob and Esau were brothers, yet says, “I loved Jacob.”
Regarding Esau, the LORD says that he hated him and turned his mountains and inheritance into a wasteland and wilderness; in the following verses, Esau is identified with Edom.
Israel will see the results of Edom’s destruction and declare that the LORD is great even beyond Israel’s borders.
The LORD expects the priests to show him honor and reverence, just as a son honors his father and a servant his master, but he accuses them of despising his name.
The priests despise the LORD by placing “defiled food” on his altar and treating the LORD’s table as something contemptible.
The priests offer blind, lame, and sick animals, and the LORD poses a moral challenge: Would they dare offer such a defective gift to a human governor?
The LORD questions whether he will show the priests favor or accept their plea, since the offerings they themselves bring before him are defective.
The LORD says he takes no pleasure in the priests’ offerings and even suggests that shutting the temple doors would be preferable to lighting his altar’s fire for no purpose.
The verse presents the greatness of the LORD’s name from east to west, and says that in every place a pure offering is presented to his name.
The priests regard altar service as a burden and even bring offerings that have been stolen, as well as lame and sick animals; the LORD asks whether he should accept such offerings from them.

The chapter concludes by condemning anyone who vows to offer a suitable animal to the LORD but sacrifices a defective one instead. It emphasizes that the LORD is a “great King” and that his name is awesome among the nations.
